fact: When James Naismith invented basketball in 1891, players used real peach baskets for hoops—someone had to climb a ladder to get the ball out after every score!
A regulation baseball has exactly 108 double stitches of red waxed thread holding its cowhide cover together.
A professional soccer player runs an average of 6 to 7 miles during a single 90-minute match.
NHL hockey pucks are frozen before every game so they glide smoothly across the ice instead of bouncing.
The New York Liberty was one of the original eight WNBA franchises when the league tipped off its very first season in 1997.
NFL footballs are nicknamed 'pigskins,' even though they have actually been made from cowhide leather for decades.
Muggsy Bogues played 14 seasons in the NBA despite standing 5 feet 3 inches tall—the shortest player in league history.
In 1920, Babe Ruth hit 54 home runs in a single season—more than every entire other team in the American League!
The five interlocking Olympic rings represent the five inhabited continents joined together by friendly competition.
The traditional black-and-white soccer ball design was created for the 1970 World Cup so viewers on black-and-white TVs could see the ball spin.
The Stanley Cup is the only major pro sports trophy where every winning player's name is engraved right onto the cup itself.
Before every Major League Baseball game, umpires rub brand-new baseballs with special Lena Blackburne mud from New Jersey so pitchers can grip them safely.
Dribbling wasn't allowed in early basketball! Players had to pass the ball from wherever they caught it.
The first Super Bowl in 1967 had thousands of empty seats—and tickets cost just $12!
A standard WNBA basketball has a slightly smaller 28.5-inch circumference than an NBA ball (29.5 inches), making ball-handling and shooting crisp.
Before penalty shootouts were invented in 1970, tied knockout soccer matches were sometimes decided by a coin flip!
At top speed, Usain Bolt's stride covered nearly 8 feet in a single step—about the length of a ping-pong table.
The longest MLB game ever played lasted 26 innings between the Brooklyn Dodgers and Boston Braves in 1920—and ended in a 1-1 tie because it got too dark!
The NBA added the 24-second shot clock in 1954 because teams used to stall by passing the ball around without shooting for minutes at a time.
Goalie masks didn't become common in the NHL until 1959, when Jacques Plante wore one after getting hit in the face by a puck.
An NFL football field is 120 yards long in total—100 yards of playing field plus two 10-yard end zones.
Soccer goalkeepers weren't required to wear a different colored jersey from their teammates until 1913.
A fastball thrown at 95 mph reaches home plate in about 0.4 seconds—barely longer than the blink of an eye.
Madison Square Garden, home of the New York Knicks, is the oldest arena in the NBA, having opened its current building in 1968.
Olympic gold medals aren't solid gold—they are actually made mostly of sterling silver plated with at least 6 grams of pure gold.
Jackie Robinson broke Major League Baseball's color barrier in 1947, and his number 42 is now retired by every MLB team.
Wayne Gretzky scored so many assists (1,963) that even if he had never scored a single goal, he would still hold the NHL all-time points record!
The 3-point line was introduced in the NBA in 1979. Chris Ford hit the very first NBA 3-pointer on October 12, 1979.
The FIFA Women's World Cup began in 1991, and the United States won the very first tournament.
The yellow first-down line you see on TV during football games isn't painted on the grass—computers draw it onto the broadcast in real time!
In 1990, Ken Griffey Sr. and Ken Griffey Jr. became the first father and son to hit back-to-back home runs in the same MLB game.
Every standard basketball hoop sits exactly 10 feet above the floor—the same height as the gym balcony where James Naismith nailed up the first peach basket.
NHL teams can play a game using more than 30 frozen pucks because pucks fly into the stands or warm up on the ice.
Mets mascot Mr. Met debuted in 1963 as a comic-book character before becoming one of the first live costumed mascots in Major League Baseball.
Yellow and red penalty cards were inspired by traffic lights—yellow means caution and red means stop!
Tug-of-war used to be an official Olympic sport from 1900 to 1920!
